comments.author: drucken
comments.why: Inventor of CAPTCHA explains how reCAPTCHA digitizes documents.
comments.text: The interesting thing about these human-based attempts to defeat individual CAPTCHA-"protected" services is that if they are actually reCAPTCHA or variants, they perform a strong socially useful function! This is because reCAPTCHA solving is linked to the digitization of paper documents. There was recently a TEDTalk by the inventor of the CAPTCHA about this topic. It is very informative and entertaining. I highly recommend it: [VIDEO]

comments.author: elviejo
comments.story: Ask HN: Could a game trick users into doing work?
comments.why: Good starting point on games with a purpose.
comments.text: Yes this is called Games with a Purpose. It is Luis Von Ahn thesis. Luis created: recaptcha, to help digitilize books by harnessing millions of captchas. The ESP game to help tag images for search purposes. Both sold to Google And later founded Duolingo, to democratize language learning. His Ted talk is a good starting point. [VIDEO]

comments.author: pittsburgh
comments.story: Google Now Using ReCAPTCHA To Decode Street View Addresses
comments.why: Luis von Ahn defends reCAPTCHA as a clever way to digitize books.
comments.text: As a developer, I agree that captchas can be a drag on users, and I think we should put serious thought into whether or not their UX-cost is justified. Personally, I try to avoid using them on sites I build. That said, as a user, it's hard to hate ReCaptcha after hearing Luis von Ahn talk about and defend his invention: [VIDEO] It's a clever way to digitize books (and now street signs) while keeping out spambots, and when I combine that knowledge with my affinity for Luis von Ahn as a person I find myself less annoyed every time I have to prove I'm not a robot.
